questions.prompt: In a finite-horizon sequence problem, the decision is
options: a single gain, used for every future time
only the first input, with the rest of the list discarded
a finite list of inputs or states, one entry for each step of the horizon
an infinite curve, with no grid and no last step
questions.explanation: The decision is the whole finite list. A single gain is a different object, used when the horizon is infinite and unconstrained. Keeping only the first input, and rebuilding later, is a later controller. An infinite curve is not a finite sequence.

questions.prompt: Three steps have stage costs \(2\), \(5\), and \(1\). What is the cost of the sequence?
questions.explanation: The cost adds one term per step: \(2 + 5 + 1 = 8\). The product \(2 \cdot 5 \cdot 1 = 10\) is not the cost. The largest stage, \(5\), leaves out the other two. A sum is the cost even when one stage is larger than the others.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 200 130" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>Three stage costs</title><text x="28" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">[</text><text x="168" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">]</text><text x="98" y="58" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">2   5   1</text></svg>
questions.figure_alt: Three stage costs written in a row.

questions.prompt: Put these steps in the order that writes a finite-horizon sequence problem.
questions.explanation: The horizon length comes first, because it fixes how long the list is. The list of that length is the decision. The stage costs and the dynamics are both written on that same list, in one step, because either statement can be written first and each only needs the list. A feasible plan is a sequence that meets the dynamics and is scored by those stage costs.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 200 130" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>Three inputs in a row</title><text x="28" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">[</text><text x="168" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">]</text><text x="98" y="58" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">u0   u1   u2</text></svg>
questions.figure_alt: A short row of decision values.
steps: Choose the number of steps in the horizon.
Name the sequence of inputs or states, of that length, as the decision.
Add a stage cost at each step of that sequence to make the objective, and write the dynamics as a constraint on the same sequence.
A feasible plan is then a sequence that meets every dynamics constraint just written, and the objective scores that sequence by its stage costs.

questions.prompt: A horizon of \(n\) steps has stage cost \(c\) at every step and a terminal cost \(p\). Write the total cost in the names n, c, and p.
questions.explanation: Each of the \(n\) steps contributes \(c\), and the terminal cost \(p\) is added once, so the total is \(nc + p\). Multiplying \(p\) by \(n\) charges the terminal cost on every step. Leaving out \(p\) drops the terminal term. A product \(ncp\) is not a sum.

questions.prompt: The update is \(x_{k+1} = x_k + u_k\), with \(x_0 = 3\) and inputs \(1\), \(-2\), \(4\). What is \(x_3\)?
questions.explanation: The state adds each input in turn: \(3 + 1 = 4\), then \(4 + (-2) = 2\), then \(2 + 4 = 6\). Stopping after the first input reports \(4\). Adding the absolute values, \(3 + 1 + 2 + 4 = 10\), flips the sign of the middle input. The dynamics are a constraint the sequence has to meet, not a cost.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 200 130" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>Three inputs in a row</title><text x="28" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">[</text><text x="168" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">]</text><text x="98" y="58" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">u0   u1   u2</text></svg>

questions.prompt: Which pieces belong in a finite-horizon sequence problem?
options: The decision is a sequence of inputs or states.
The cost adds a term along that sequence.
The dynamics constrain which sequences are feasible.
Only the first input is kept, and the problem is rebuilt at the next sample.
questions.explanation: The decision is the sequence, the cost is a sum along it, and the dynamics are constraints. Rebuilding at the next sample, and keeping only the first input, is a later controller. It is not part of writing the one sequence.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 200 130" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>Three inputs in a row</title><text x="28" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">[</text><text x="168" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">]</text><text x="98" y="58" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">u0   u1   u2</text></svg>
questions.figure_alt: A short row of decision values.

questions.prompt: A note writes a finite-horizon problem. Exactly one step is wrong.
questions.explanation: The dynamics are constraints. They do not replace the sum. The list of inputs is the decision, the sum of stage terms is the cost, and a sequence that breaks the update is rejected. Calling the dynamics the objective drops the cost.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 200 130" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>Three inputs in a row</title><text x="28" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">[</text><text x="168" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">]</text><text x="98" y="58" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">u0   u1   u2</text></svg>
questions.figure_alt: A short row of decision values.
steps: The decision is the list of inputs over the finite horizon.
The cost adds one stage term for each step.
The dynamics replace that sum and become the objective.
A sequence that breaks the update is not feasible.
reasons: The dynamics are constraints, and the sum stays the cost.
The decision should be a single gain instead of a list.
A sequence that breaks the update is still feasible.

questions.prompt: The inputs on three steps are \(3\), \(1\), and \(1\). What is the energy, the sum of the squared inputs?
questions.explanation: Square each input and add: \(9 + 1 + 1 = 11\). The sum of the inputs themselves is \(5\), which drops the squares. The product of the squares is \(9\), which is not a sum. Energy here is one kind of stage cost, still a sum along the sequence.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 200 130" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>Three inputs</title><text x="28" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">[</text><text x="168" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">]</text><text x="98" y="58" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">3   1   1</text></svg>
questions.figure_alt: Three inputs written in a row.

questions.prompt: A dynamics constraint on a finite sequence means
options: a candidate list is feasible only when each next state matches the update
the cost of every feasible list is zero
the horizon has to be infinite
the stage costs are multiplied instead of added
questions.explanation: The update ties each state to the previous state and the input. A list that breaks that tie is not feasible. The cost of a feasible list can still be positive. The horizon stays finite. The stage costs are still added.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 200 130" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>Three inputs in a row</title><text x="28" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">[</text><text x="168" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">]</text><text x="98" y="58" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">u0   u1   u2</text></svg>
questions.figure_alt: A short row of decision values.

questions.prompt: Samples of one coordinate sit at \(0\), \(2\), and \(5\). What is the smoothness cost, the sum of the squared steps between consecutive samples?
questions.explanation: The steps are \(2 - 0 = 2\) and \(5 - 2 = 3\). The squared lengths are \(4\) and \(9\), and the sum is \(13\). Adding the positions, \(0 + 2 + 5 = 7\), is not a sum of steps. A later skill keeps this sum and adds an obstacle that can make the feasible set nonconvex.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 200 130" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>Three samples on a line</title><text x="28" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">[</text><text x="168" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">]</text><text x="98" y="58" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">0   2   5</text></svg>
questions.figure_alt: Three sample positions written in a row.

questions.prompt: A later controller solves a short sequence from the current state and applies only the first input. Compared with the problem in this skill, that controller
options: drops the sum, because a sequence cannot have a cost
rebuilds the sequence at the next sample instead of keeping one open-loop list
removes the dynamics, because a constraint cannot be written on a sequence
replaces the sequence by one gain computed for an infinite horizon
questions.explanation: This skill decides the whole list once. The later controller throws the tail away and writes the problem again at the next sample. The sum and the dynamics stay available in both problems. An infinite-horizon gain is a different object again.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 200 130" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>Three inputs in a row</title><text x="28" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">[</text><text x="168" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">]</text><text x="98" y="58" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">u0   u1   u2</text></svg>
questions.figure_alt: A short row of decision values.

questions.prompt: A horizon has \(7\) steps, and each step has one input. How many inputs are in the decision?
questions.explanation: One input per step gives a list of length \(7\). A count of \(6\) drops the last step. A count of \(8\) adds an input past the horizon. A later controller may apply only the first of these seven and rebuild; this question asks how long the list is.
